analysis.one_liner: Freezes big agribusiness mergers for 18 months and creates a commission to study farm-market concentration.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after its sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors introduced it, it was sent to House committees and four subcommittees and sat there until the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped large agribusiness firms — big meatpackers, grain processors, and farm-input sellers — from buying or merging with each other for up to 18 months, with waivers only in extraordinary cases like a company's insolvency. It would also have created a 12-member commission to study concentration in farm markets and recommend changes to antitrust laws. The stated goal was to slow the consolidation that the bill's findings said was squeezing family farmers and rural communities. It was referred to House committees, then to four Agriculture subcommittees, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers, who would face fewer dominant buyers for their crops and livestock; rural communities dependent on farm income; and potentially food shoppers, since the bill's findings said low farm prices were not being passed on at the supermarket. Small and mid-sized agribusiness firms would also face a pause in competition from ever-larger rivals.

how_it_helps.text: For up to 18 months, agribusiness firms with over $100 million in sales or assets would be barred from merging with or acquiring other large agribusiness entities, halting new consolidation while Congress considered broader legislation [S2][S3].

A 12-member commission, required to include sitting farmers and ranchers, would study concentration across the food chain and recommend changes to antitrust law to keep markets fair for small and medium producers [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cited steep concentration — the top four beef packers reaching 80% of the market, the farmer's share of the retail food dollar falling below 25% — as the problem the freeze and commission were meant to address [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness corporations — meatpackers, grain processors, agricultural input suppliers, and dealers — which would be blocked from acquisitions for up to 18 months and face a commission likely to recommend tougher antitrust enforcement. Taxpayers would fund the commission, authorized at $2 million.

drawbacks.text: A blanket freeze would also stop mergers that could be procompetitive or that rescue financially distressed firms; the Attorney General's waiver covers only extraordinary cases like insolvency, so even questionable-but-legal deals would be blocked [S3].

The moratorium was temporary — expiring at the earlier of 18 months or comprehensive concentration legislation — and a study commission does not itself restore competition; without follow-on legislation the freeze would lapse and consolidation could resume [S2][S3].
The commission and its staff were authorized at $2 million in appropriations, a cost to taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a genuine, if temporary, brake on consolidation in markets where a handful of firms bought from farmers, and it required the commission to include working farmers. But it was a pause rather than a fix: an 18-month freeze plus a study commission would not itself unwind existing concentration, and the moratorium's rigidity — with waivers limited to insolvency — could block deals that made sense. It died before any of these tradeoffs were tested in a committee markup or floor debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture and Judiciary Committees and then to four Agriculture subcommittees, and no committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl Pomeroy introduced the bill on October 27, 1999, joined by Reps. David Minge and Tammy Baldwin, and it drew five Democratic cosponsors in total [S1][S3][S4][S5].
The Speaker referred it to both the Agriculture Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

On November 3, 1999, the Agriculture Committee sent it to four of its subcommittees, and executive comment was requested from USDA — steps that typically precede, and often replace, serious consideration [S5].
No hearing, markup, or vote is recorded; the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large agribusiness firms — the major meatpackers, grain processors, and farm-input companies — were free to continue merging and acquiring, with no freeze and no commission to review concentration. Family farmers and rural communities gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so the record shows no roll calls revealing whether the fight would have split by party.

industries.note: The bill's findings said the top four beef packers controlled 80% of the market and the top four pork packers 57%, and the moratorium would have stopped further acquisitions by these firms. Their bargaining power over farmers — and the bill's claim that low farm prices were not passed on to shoppers — is exactly what the freeze targeted [S3].

Large input sellers with over $100 million in sales would have been barred from acquiring rivals for up to 18 months. Farmers buying seed, fertilizer, and chemicals from an ever-smaller set of suppliers were the intended beneficiaries of the pause [S2][S3].
The moratorium expressly exempted cooperatives and entities owned by them, leaving co-ops free to combine while their corporate rivals were frozen [S3].

industries.industry: Grain dealers, brokers, and warehouse operators
industries.note: Large dealers, commission merchants, brokers, and warehouse operators above the bill's size thresholds would have been blocked from acquisitions during the moratorium [S3].
